item.title: From code to content: How AI could make India the world’s next story exporter
item.description: Eloelo Group’s Saurabh Pandey showcased Dolphin AI, an end-to-end video production suite, and told TechSparks 2026 that falling production costs could let Indian storytellers compete for global audiences.
item.content:encoded:
India spent the 1990s and 2000s becoming the back office of the world for code. At TechSparks 2026, a flagship event of YourStory, one founder asked whether the country can now do the same for stories. As AI makes video production more efficient and economical, his answer was a confident yes.

The session, titled ‘Can AI turn India into a global content export hub?’, began with the product showcase of Dolphin AI by Saurabh Pandey, Founder and CEO of Eloelo Group, and then moved into a fireside chat with Shradha Sharma, Founder and CEO of YourStory and The Bharat Project.

Why India has not yet exported its stories

Pandey noted that India has long produced standout IPs such as Baahubali, Kantara, and RRR, but has rarely been an exporter. Japan did it with anime, South Korea with K-dramas, China with micro dramas, and the US with Hollywood. Each, he said, used content to build soft power.

AI, in his view, changes the equation because the tools once available only to a few markets are now open to everyone. The opportunity also goes beyond films, to localized advertisements, commerce videos, and social media content for overseas customers.

Dolphin AI: One suite from idea to final cut

To make that case concrete, Pandey introduced Dolphin AI, Eloelo’s newest launch. The company began with live entertainment, moved into micro dramas with its Story TV app, and recently added a micro learning app called Master.

Dolphin AI targets a familiar creator hurdle: making one AI video often means stitching together clips and edits from around 20 tools. Dolphin AI replaces that with an agentic chat and a set of templates. A simple prompt can produce a full video, with the suite handling context and continuity. It also integrates with Claude and ChatGPT through MCP, helping creators build longer AI videos. A short demo reel closed the showcase.

Fireside chat: Removing the gatekeepers

When Sharma joined Pandey on stage, she reacted to the demo with pride. “This is remarkable. This is real, and this is happening in India,” she said.

The conversation first turned to adoption. Pandey said roughly 15,000 videos were created on Dolphin AI in eight days in its early access phase, entirely through organic discovery.

He then explained why this matters for storytellers. High-end visual effects once meant massive budgets, and those budgets acted as a filter on who could tell ambitious stories.

“With AI, with tools such as Dolphin AI, what we are trying to build is that you can ship content without any gatekeepers,” he said. He clarified that AI is not replacing actors but expensive locations, so a period drama no longer needs a real palace. With distribution now largely algorithmic, a storyteller in India can reach audiences in the US or Europe.

Asked why India has lagged, Pandey did not blame creativity. He compared South Korea, with 52 million people and a content export economy of about $15 billion, to India’s 1.4 billion.

“I would refuse to believe that we don’t have the creativity,” he said. In his view, technology, aspiration, distribution and capital must come together, and Indian builders have too often treated the local market as the only one that matters.

The micro drama moment

On whether micro dramas can finally work as a business in India, Pandey cited China, where the category reached roughly $8 billion in revenue last year and is now at a run rate of $10 billion to $11 billion, with a single platform earning more than China’s entire box office. In India, he said, the combined run rate of the top four or five players is north of Rs 5,000 crore, reached in about 18 months.

Production costs have been the stumbling block, historically eating up 50-60% of revenue. AI, he argued, finally fixes the supply side. “This is that quick commerce moment of entertainment,” he said.

Where the opportunity sits

Pandey expects platforms to consolidate around two or three players, as food delivery and ecommerce did. Supply, however, will stay open. Eloelo launched 200 new micro dramas last month for its microdrama platform Story TV and works with about 90 production houses, a number he sees doubling.

His advice for new entrants was to build on the supply side. Small, nimble AI studios of a few editors, promo producers and a line producer could supply platforms with micro dramas and OTT content. He urged writers and producers to treat AI as a brainstorming partner, and floated the idea of an AI-made Mahabharat.

“The next Disney or the next big IP can be built now if the right supply engine comes in because the demand is very clear,” he said.

The window to build

Pandey said Eloelo, which has grown from one platform to five, is not eyeing an IPO soon and is focused on sustainable growth while it builds for India’s global ambitions.

Sharma called his journey from a Flipkart employee to founder building for the world a reminder of what Indian aspiration can achieve. She urged the audience to tell their teams and networks that the window to build in this space is open. If India turned code into a global export, the session suggested, stories could be next.

item.title: WOI India launches venture studios, investor network, and startup support platforms at TechSparks 2026
item.description: WOI India introduced platforms focused on venture building, sales, marketing, and ecommerce, along with an investor network and a Founder Card connecting entrepreneurs to the Startup Park ecosystem.
item.content:encoded:
Building a startup takes more than a good idea. Founders need capital, teams, market access, and practical support to turn their plans into businesses. At TechSparks 2026, WOI India launched a set of platforms aimed at addressing these needs, from venture studios that work alongside founders to services focused on sales, marketing, and investor connections.

Amar Dixit, CEO of WOI India, led the launch with a video showcasing the organization’s existing initiatives and long-term plans.

WOI India is the Indian arm of Dubai-headquartered WOI, a global ecosystem-development company. Its model covers infrastructure, capital, education, venture studios, community, and Centres of Excellence. Its flagship Startup Park in Bengaluru provides founders with access to workspace, mentorship, capital, and other support.

Dixit invited entrepreneurs to visit Startup Park, an integrated hub and community centre in Koramangala, Bengaluru. He also outlined plans to expand the model, with more startup parks in the pipeline.

Dayone Venture Studio: Building alongside founders

Mazin Arbaz, Founder of Dayone Venture Studio, introduced the platform by addressing a common challenge for entrepreneurs: mentors can offer guidance and investors can provide capital, but who helps founders build their businesses?

Operating under WOI, Dayone was founded by Arbaz, with Hashir Usman as CEO. The studio combines investment with hands-on support, working with startups from their early stages to turn ideas into viable businesses.

Its work covers understanding customers, building brands, setting up systems and making the decisions needed to move a business forward.

At TechSparks, Arbaz invited founders with business ideas, investors interested in co-building ventures and professionals looking to work with the studio to get in touch.

Dayone aims to combine funding with practical business-building support, helping founders navigate the early stages of setting up and growing a company.

Perform100X: Helping startups drive sales and marketing

For Krishnakumar V, Co-founder and CEO of Perform100X, and Shanfaz C K M, Co-founder and Chief Strategy Officer, sales is a challenge startups need to address early.

Perform100X is a sales and marketing accelerator operating as a Centre of Excellence. It brings together talent, strategy, technology, and execution to help startups turn products into customers, revenue, and sustainable growth.

The platform aims to offer an alternative to working with multiple agencies and managing disconnected marketing activities.

Its services include market analysis, data-backed planning, technology-enabled execution, and performance dashboards.

Analyticsfy, its intelligence layer, brings reporting and performance insights into a single dashboard. Founders can access information through simple WhatsApp commands.

Speaking at TechSparks, Krishnakumar said the team had spent the previous two days networking with founders and found that sales was one of the biggest challenges startups faced after raising investment.

Perform100X aims to work as an extension of a startup’s team, aligning sales and marketing activities with its valuation criteria and investment plans.

Krishnakumar also highlighted the platform’s reporting capabilities, which give founders visibility into strategies and execution without having to wait until the end of the month to assess performance.

Point Zero: Supporting early-stage ecommerce brands

Arshak N, Founder of Point Zero, introduced the venture studio, which aims to help Indian ecommerce brands navigate their early stages, when founders often lack the team, direction, and capital needed to get started.

Point Zero works alongside entrepreneurs as a co-founder, providing a team, capital, expertise in brand building, product development, growth and operations, and shared playbooks.

Founders can bring their own ideas to build founder-led ventures or lead studio-born brands developed through Point Zero’s research.

The studio focuses on building brands with products that encourage repeat purchases, margins that can support growth, and a reason for customers to buy beyond price.

It is mentored by brand builders including Bharat Sethi of Rage Coffee and Palash Arneja of BlaBliBlu.

At TechSparks, Arshak said many ecommerce founders spend their first year building businesses alone, even though this is often when they need the most support.

Point Zero aims to provide the teams, playbooks, capital, and direction needed to build and grow these businesses.

Launched at TechSparks, the studio has set a target of achieving Rs 1,000 crore in combined revenue across its portfolio within the next three years.

Applications are open to founders and investors interested in building ecommerce brands.

VC Circle: Building a global investor network

Hema Harshini, Business Head at VC Circle by WOI, is leading the platform's efforts to build a global network connecting investors, intelligence and opportunities across markets.

VC Circle brings together fund managers, venture funds, family offices, high-net-worth individuals and institutional investors.

Through curated roundtables, demo days, investor-focused reports and ecosystem engagements, it aims to help participants exchange ideas, identify emerging sectors and explore investment opportunities.

At TechSparks, Harshini spoke about the platform’s first chapter, which included a roundtable on commercializing India’s next space economy.

The discussion brought together government and industry representatives, including participants from NSIL, WICCI, COS and the Space Tech Foundation, alongside investors such as C Fund and Ivy Capital.

VC Circle also launched its first report based on the roundtable, along with a magazine. Both were available at the TechSparks Startup Park booth.

Harshini said the larger goal was to build a globally connected investor ecosystem that brings together capital, relationships, and intelligence to identify and develop opportunities.

Founder Card: Connecting entrepreneurs to Startup Park

Arun Das Janadaran, CEO of Startup Park, introduced Founder Card, a platform designed to help entrepreneurs access the wider startup ecosystem.

Aimed at founders at different stages, Founder Card connects members with workspaces, mentorship, learning opportunities, investor networks, and other resources to help them build and scale their businesses.

At TechSparks, Janadaran said successful entrepreneurs need more than ideas. They also need people, knowledge, and opportunities to turn those ideas into businesses.

Founder Card, he explained, aims to make Startup Park’s ecosystem more accessible, giving entrepreneurs opportunities to connect, collaborate, and grow.

With these launches, WOI India is bringing venture building, sales and marketing support, ecommerce development, investor connections and founder resources together within its startup ecosystem.

item.title: antimattr is building voice AI wearables that cut through the noise
item.description: Backed by YC and WTFund, San Francisco-based antimattr is building wearable tech for human-agent interaction that summarises conversations with clarity in noisy environments.
item.content:encoded:
When Sridipto Ghosh and Sirsha Chakraborty were developing the thesis for their startup, many advised them against venturing into hardware. But this didn’t deter them.

“People said it was hard, that there were large companies in the hardware space, and that it was very difficult for a startup to build in this space. We continued building despite those perceptions,” says Ghosh.

Their persistence eventually led them to start antimattr in 2025. The deeptech company is building a voice-first hardware interface for human-agent interaction that summarises conversations with clarity even in noisy environments.

The conversations could be with anyone. Users can dictate to the wearable device directly or let it listen to a conversation with another person (offline or online). The technology would be able to pick up the conversation clearly despite ambient noise, says CEO Ghosh.

He says its early incubation at Scaler Innovation Lab helped the startup get off the ground. “It gave us access to prototyping equipment such as 3D printers and soldering stations, which made it easier to iterate and keep developing the idea."

The name ‘antimattr’ comes from the philosophy of challenging common notions or what people are generally taught. This year, the San Francisco-based startup was selected for Y Combinator’s current cohort, becoming the first India-origin wearable company backed by the accelerator.

“One of our biggest learnings so far has been that you don’t need to have everything figured out before you start. You just need to keep moving and evolving. YC has accelerated this process for us at a global stage and pushed us further in thinking about what’s possible in human-machine interaction,” says Ghosh.

Also Read
Peak XV selects 18 startups for 12th Surge cohort, doubles down on AI and deep tech

Wearable tech that is noise-proof

One of antimattr’s projects is project mnemosyne, a voice-first hardware interface for human-to-agent (H2A) communication.

Chakraborty, the startup’s CTO, says the barrier to adopting voice AI is not technical but the reality of noisy environments, where voice is not always usable.

“For instance, dictating with clarity and accuracy while sitting in a noisy cafe is generally not possible. We are building an interface that makes voice usable everywhere, makes using it private, and solves H2A communication,” he says.

The startup’s system pairs a ring with earphones. The earphones use proprietary voice isolation technology to block out background noise, allowing users to take a call from a loud place, such as a pub, or dictate with greater accuracy. The ring runs the software by capturing thoughts, controlling agents, and summarising conversations.

Beyond this, the startup’s roadmap includes project soteria and project athena.

The team believes the future of personal AI will be private and not dependent on the cloud—a private, local computer can run all your models and have all your context.

“The next milestone towards this vision is project soteria, as true freedom begins with privacy and ownership. The final frontier for antimattr is project athena, which we envision as the machine that defines how humans function,” he says.

Chakraborty says antimattr’s long-term vision is to build an ecosystem of devices for natural human-machine interaction.

Also Read
Deeptech is giving rise to new kinds of founders and bold ideas: VCs

Unlike the general assumption, antimattr’s products are not always listening to humans. They record only when users deliberately trigger them. The CTO says the team retains the raw audio but does not use it to train any model.

“We are currently pursuing SOC 2 and HIPAA compliance to bring enterprise-grade security to how data is stored and handled,” he says.

Ghosh says more than 500 customers have placed pre-orders through its website. The beta version of mnemosyne is expected to launch publicly by December this year.

The founders initially invested about Rs 25 lakh in the startup. They recently received a Rs 20 lakh equity-free grant from Nikhil Kamath’s WTFund.

antimattr competes with startups such as San Francisco-based Bee. Ghosh says antimattr’s edge lies in its focus on the real-world challenges of using voice AI in noisy environments.

“Nobody wants to shout at AI or be overheard. Even companies building hardware aren’t solving this ground-up for voice. We are building a full-stack interface that is tuned for voice and allows users to use voice anywhere,” Ghosh says.

Edited by Swetha Kannan

item.title: Crypto’s next chapter: Regulatory sandboxes, AI co-pilots and the rise of derivatives
item.description: At TechSparks 2026, Rajagopal Menon of WazirX, Satish Mishra of Pi42 and SharkExchange, and Sharat Chandra of EmpowerEdge Ventures discussed how regulation, risk management and AI are reshaping crypto investing in India
item.content:encoded:
Crypto investing is evolving beyond its early hype cycles. Regulation, investor awareness, risk management and new technologies are changing how people trade digital assets, all while raising pertinent questions about what responsible participation should look like.

At TechSparks 2026, Rajagopal Menon, Vice President at WazirX; Satish Mishra, CTO of Pi42 and SharkExchange; and Sharat Chandra, Founder of EmpowerEdge Ventures, joined Swetha Kannan, Deputy Editor at YourStory, to discuss the changing crypto landscape, the need for regulatory clarity, and the growing role of AI in trading.

A new crypto landscape emerges

India’s crypto market has historically been a dynamic space, growing rapidly during the 2021-22 bull run, where Menon noted that WazirX’s spot markets processed close to $48 billion in transactions during that period. This was succeeded by the taxation measures introduced in the subsequent Budget that changed the market significantly.

According to Menon, the resulting environment of these changes has placed Indian exchanges at a disadvantage compared with foreign platforms. Domestic exchanges must deduct tax at source (TDS) and operate within the 30% tax framework, while foreign exchanges have not faced the same requirements, he argued. “I think a stable environment or a better environment would be that the same rules apply for everybody, so that Make in India is made for Indian exchanges,” he shared.

Menon also pointed to a shift in trading activity. As spot trading volumes declined, futures and derivatives began gaining traction. He expects this segment to see significant adoption in India.

Regulation that makes room for all players

Moving to the question of regulation, Chandra shared that exchanges had helped educate investors about different crypto assets and the importance of understanding risks, but that gaps in the regulatory framework remained. “I think once this space is regulated, that can lead to a lot of capital inflow to the country,” he said.

Chandra pointed out that while exchanges are required to follow KYC norms, there are still gaps when it comes to verifying identities as assets move on-chain. He suggested that regulatory sandboxes could help address some of these challenges. SEBI and IFSCA already have sandboxes to encourage innovation in the capital markets, but digital asset native fintech players have not yet been given the go-ahead to participate.

He also highlighted the potential of tokenisation, pointing to the tokenisation of corporate bonds as an example. For now, participation is limited to institutional players. Chandra suggested that opening up regulatory sandboxes to more web3 fintech companies could help them test new ideas, improve existing processes and play a bigger role in the tokenisation journey.

Crypto infrastructure: Built for endurance

Unlike traditional financial markets, crypto trades 24 hours a day, seven days a week. For tech teams, that means monitoring systems, managing risk and responding to incidents without the predictable downtime offered by market closing hours.

Mishra described how trading activity on crypto platforms can pick up during evenings and weekends, partly in response to movements in US markets. This places continuous demands on observability, alerts and leverage monitoring.

His experience building a spot trading exchange also showed how quickly demand for derivatives can outpace infrastructure development. At Pi42, the team took a different approach from the outset, building a platform specifically for derivatives rather than adapting a spot-trading system.

Production incidents, Mishra noted, had occurred over weekends when systems could not keep pace with demand. The experience underlined the need to build infrastructure around crypto’s round-the-clock operating model.

Beyond the hype: When risk management is embedded in processes

As more people enter the crypto market, investor education and effective compliance become increasingly important. Menon pointed to WazirX’s ‘Gangs of Cryptopur’ campaign, which aims to help investors understand what they’re trading. He also spoke about taking a disciplined approach to crypto, comparing the historical returns of different asset classes with Bitcoin. His advice was to think long term rather than treat crypto as a series of short-term bets.

For exchanges, making the process easier for users is just as important as maintaining compliance checks. Mishra explained that KYC can be frustrating when an application fails and users have to start all over again. Technology can make this simpler by letting users pick up where they left off and clearly explaining what needs to be corrected.

He added that genuine users are generally less likely to be bothered by compliance checks than those trying to get around them. The aim is to make the process smoother for users while retaining the checks needed to identify suspicious activity.

Putting AI to work in crypto: regulation, education, innovation

AI is also changing how traders research markets and assess potential trades. Menon said WazirX has introduced an AI-powered feature that scans more than 300 tokens to spot those showing bearish momentum. WazirX AI - India’s first AI-powered crypto agent is a conversational co-pilot that handles advanced, multi-step requests, including technical indicators such as the Moving Average Convergence Divergence (MACD) and Relative Strength Index (RSI), and offers recommendations for users to consider. Traders must confirm their chosen strategy before the AI places an order with stop-loss and take-profit parameters.

Menon sees AI as a way to analyse large volumes of market data and spot patterns, but he also highlighted that AI should support decisions rather than make them for users.

Mishra also urged traders to backtest AI-generated strategies and monitor their performance before using them in live markets, saying “If you ask AI to give you a strategy and then run with it, make sure that you are also observing it so as soon as it goes wrong, you can unplug it.”

Chandra noted that regulatory implications will depend on how AI is used. Educational tools could be treated differently from systems that offer personalised investment advice, which could fall under investment-adviser regulations. He also stressed the need for AI systems to be trustworthy, explainable, auditable and fair.

What comes next for crypto?

As the crypto landscape changes with new regulations, AI disruptions and evolving investor expectations, Menon, Chandra and Mishra were asked what would represent the next phase of the sector.

For Menon, it was futures and derivatives. Mishra agreed, noting that derivatives have continued to grow and address specific needs within the crypto ecosystem.

Chandra pointed to another emerging possibility: compute futures, with developments such as the launch of compute futures by CME in the US indicating how new asset classes could emerge at the intersection of AI and digital assets.

As the market evolves, the discussion highlighted three interconnected priorities: clearer regulation, stronger infrastructure and more informed use of AI. The next phase of crypto investing in India will depend not just on new products and trading opportunities, but also on how effectively the ecosystem manages risk and builds trust.

item.title: Why AI-powered intelligence is every winning brand’s secret sauce
item.description: As AI reshapes ecommerce, brands are shifting focus from customer acquisition to intelligent fulfilment, inventory management and customer experience. The article explores how AI and agentic systems enable smarter, faster operational decisions.
item.content:encoded:
For years, the playbook for building a winning consumer brand was simple: a compelling product, a strong brand identity, and smart customer acquisition. Those fundamentals still hold, but they no longer decide who wins.

Today's battle is fought in fragments of attention, where brands have seconds to convert interest into a purchase. And the moment “Buy Now” is clicked, a second, harder battle begins: fast fulfilment, a seamless delivery experience, and effortless handling of queries and returns - the moments that actually earn loyalty.

Amid endless channels and ever-shifting marketing strategies, the real differentiator has moved downstream: it's the intelligence behind every operational decision made after the click.

Artificial intelligence is rapidly becoming this intelligence layer. No longer limited to chatbots or content generation, AI is transforming how brands forecast demand, allocate inventory, orchestrate fulfilment, engage customers, and optimise operations in real time.

This shift comes at a time when commerce itself has grown far more complex. Consumers now discover, evaluate, and buy across a maze of touchpoints - brand websites, marketplaces, quick commerce, social commerce, and physical stores - often within a single purchase journey. Powering every one of those purchases is a complex web of inventory nodes, warehouses, logistics partners, and engagement systems that must move in perfect synchronisation.

For brands, this translates into a flood of operational data. Every inventory movement, customer interaction, order update, warehouse scan, and delivery milestone becomes a signal that can influence the next business decision. What begins as a simple online business quickly turns into a web of real-time, interconnected decisions - each one shaping the customer experience.

Until a few years ago, brands and marketplaces operated on Systems of Record - a single source of operational truth that captured transactions and helped manage inventory. Ecommerce enablement SaaS platforms turned these Systems of Insight - real-time dashboards and analytics that let businesses move from reactive to data-driven decision-making.

The next phase of this evolution is now underway. Building on this rich data and technology-enabled processes, these Systems of Record and Insight are becoming Systems of Intelligence - where AI is not just analysing information, but actively framing recommendations and executing decisions across business operations.

Consider a fashion retailer during a festive sale. Thousands of orders may arrive simultaneously across its website, marketplaces, and quick commerce platforms. Instead of relying on manual rules or static workflows, AI can continuously evaluate inventory availability, warehouse capacity, delivery timelines, shipping costs, and customer location before automatically routing each order through the most efficient fulfilment path. It can also spot that a fast-moving product is about to run out in one city while stock sits healthy elsewhere and line up a transfer before availability ever becomes the customer's problem.

This matters even more in an omnichannel world, where customers expect availability wherever and however they shop. Delivering on that promise takes more than inventory visibility - it demands continuous coordination across allocation, order orchestration, warehouse operations, logistics, and customer communication. AI makes that coordination possible at a scale and speed manual decision-making simply can't match.

The next frontier here is Agentic AI. Unlike traditional automation, which follows predefined workflows, Agentic AI can reason across multiple variables, recommend the next best course of action, and autonomously execute routine operational decisions within business-defined guardrails. Whether prioritising high-value orders during peak demand, responding to supply chain disruptions, or flagging fulfilment bottlenecks before they bite, these systems move beyond supporting human decisions to actively driving them.

This marks a fundamental shift in how brands approach growth. Acquiring customers remains critical, but sustainable growth increasingly depends on what happens after demand is generated. Rather than adding operational headcount every time order volumes spike, businesses are investing in intelligent platforms that let them scale without proportionately scaling complexity. The goal is no longer simply to process more orders - it's to make better operational decisions, faster and more consistently.

Ecommerce enablement platforms, with deep data and operational ties into brands, are already building this future. AI-first SaaS tools are no longer just software - they're becoming operational partners, continuously improving how the business runs.

Tomorrow's market leaders won't necessarily be the brands with the biggest marketing budgets. They'll be the brands whose technology lets them operate smarter, adapt faster, and make better decisions every single day. Their competitive advantage will increasingly come from the intelligence behind every business decision they make.

(Kapil Makhija is the MD & CEO of Unicommerce eSolutions Limited)

item.title: From prompt engineers to tool builders: Intuit’s Vignesh Subrahmaniam on building AI that acts
item.description: At TechSparks 2026, Intuit’s Principal AI Scientist explained why reliable tools, high-quality data, and consent matter more than ever as AI moves from answering to acting
item.content:encoded:
For the past few years, getting better results from AI meant learning to write better prompts. That is changing fast, as AI systems begin to reason, make decisions, and act across entire workflows on their own.

At TechSparks 2026, YourStory’s flagship event, Dr Vignesh Subrahmaniam, Principal AI Scientist at Intuit, spoke with Adith Charlie, Managing Editor of YourStory and The CapTable, in a fireside chat titled ‘Beyond the prompt: Building AI that thinks, acts, learns’. Drawing on Subrahmaniam's experience of turning AI research into scalable systems, the two explored what builders need to rethink as intelligence becomes increasingly agentic.

Teaching machines the game of business

The session opened with a question for Subrahmaniam about what a typical day looks like for him. He was also asked to simplify the concepts of fintech and AI for the audience. He responded with a chess analogy, posing a question: if an algorithm were never taught the rules of chess but was shown a million completed games and their winners, could it deduce both the rules and the strategies most likely to lead to victory? His team at Intuit applies a similar approach to supporting small businesses, as the company serves both consumers and accountants. 

“How do we learn the game of business by looking at data, by looking at actual actions and outcomes that businesses are taking,” he said. The goal is to understand what helps a business win customers, grow quickly, and improve its cash flow.

From prompts to tools

The conversation then turned to the shift builders face, from years of learning to write smarter prompts to designing agents that are handed a goal and decide the steps themselves.

Subrahmaniam placed prompt engineering in the long history of programming languages, from binary and assembly to Fortran, C, and Python. Large language models let anyone program using plain English. However, this method has limits. Researchers quickly understood that intelligence should not only be in the model.

The model becomes an orchestrator, breaking a complex task into a series of actions and tool calls. The real intelligence moves into the tools it calls. Those tools must be built differently too, “not so that a human being can use them, or a software developer can use them, or anybody can use them, but in a way that an LLM orchestrator can really use them”.

That means high-fidelity tools with highly deterministic output. For builders, the craft shifts from clever wording to dependable components that a model can call on again and again without surprises.

The next frontier is beyond text

On where new data will come from, Subrahmaniam was candid that learning from text is now largely a solved problem. The harder challenge is learning from multimodal sources and real-world actions. He pointed to how a small child learns mostly from what she sees, hears and observes, not from reading, and argued that bringing such real-world signals into AI systems is what will help models go beyond generating text to suggesting actions. That, he said, is the next frontier.

Data quality still decides everything

Looking ahead at the challenges for a regulated industry, he took the audience back 18 years, to one of the first machine learning labs in Bangalore, where he worked on logistic regressions and multi-layer perceptrons. The biggest problem then was not the algorithm. “Actually, it was data quality,” he recalled.

That has not changed. Whether a team trains a simple regression or fine-tunes a transformer, “garbage in, garbage out” still applies. Enterprises that can collect, collate, and store data at the highest quality, he said, will have the edge.

Consent and privacy from the floor

In the short audience Q&A, an attendee asked how restrictions on where financial data can be stored affect Intuit’s work. Subrahmaniam called consent the heart of any learning system and cited the Framingham study, where residents of a Massachusetts town allowed doctors to follow their health over time, which shaped modern understanding of cardiovascular disease. 

Companies, he added, must also explain the benefits of data use to the wider community. 

What builders can take away

As the conversation drew to a close, one thread ran through every answer: as AI moves from responding to acting, the foundations matter more than the interface. 

Prompts will remain a starting point, but the real work now lies in building dependable tools that agents can call on, feeding systems high-quality data, and earning the consent that lets them learn from it. 

For builders looking beyond the prompt, that is where the next wave of AI will be won.

item.title: Beyond funding: Why every startup founder needs an insurance plan
item.description:
From personal term insurance to keyman and employee cover, here's how insurance solutions can help entrepreneurs protect their families, businesses, and teams.
Most founders are equity-rich and cash-poor, with household finances quietly tied to the venture: personal guarantees on business loans
item.content:encoded:
Most founders are equity-rich and cash-poor, with household finances quietly tied to the venture: personal guarantees on business loans, savings deployed into the company, a spouse’s income covering monthly basics. That structure makes personal term insurance more urgent for a founder than for a salaried peer, not less. If the founder dies, the family inherits illiquid equity and live liabilities at the same moment, and only a large, immediate payout resolves that.

The sizing rule also needs adjusting. The standard guidance of 10-15X annual income understates the need for entrepreneurs who deliberately pay themselves a modest salary. Anchor instead to household expenses, outstanding personal guarantees, and the real cost of the family’s next 15 years. Self-employed applicants should expect income documentation requests, ITRs, and bank statements rather than salary slips, and treat that as an administrative step rather than a reason to postpone.

What Does ABSLI Super Term Plan Offer a Founder?

The payout structure matters for founders carrying loan guarantees. A lump sum clears liabilities at once, while the monthly income option keeps a household running for a defined period, and ABSLI Super Term Plan allows the two to be combined, with between 10% and 90% of the sum assured taken as income and the balance as a lump sum.

What is keyman insurance and who needs it?

Ask your co-founder a direct question: if either of you died this quarter, does the company survive the next funding conversation? Investors ask themselves the same thing, which is why keyman insurance appears in diligence checklists and shareholder agreements.

ABSLI Keyman Insurance Policy is a life insurance policy purchased by an employer on the life of a key employee, based on the insurable interest an employer has in that person. The payout gives the business capital to stabilise, hire replacement leadership, and reassure the cap table at the moment confidence is scarcest.

For partnership firms, ABSLI Partnership Insurance Scheme addresses a related risk: on the death of an insured partner, the firm has liquidity available to purchase the deceased partner’s share, so working capital is not diverted and surviving partners are not required to bring in additional funds. Cover is assessed against the firm’s net worth, including each partner’s share of capital, share of profit and share in goodwill.

How does employer-employee cover work for a startup team?

This is the part that belongs in your next HR planning cycle. Under ABSLI Employer - Employee Insurance Scheme, the employer proposes and owns a policy on the life of an employee, and assigns it to the employee after a defined period. Assignment can be absolute, transferring ownership at issuance, or conditional, transferring ownership once terms set by the employer are met. Any company, proprietorship firm, LLP, trust, NGO or society with a genuine employer-employee relationship is eligible.

The return on that spend is talent economics. Startups ask employees to accept risk, and benefits that protect an employee’s family are how a company signals it takes that trade seriously. The structure also matures with the company: the arrangement that covers a handful of employees becomes the foundation of the full benefits programme a later-stage HR lead will build. All products other than child plans can be offered under the scheme, and all riders other than Waiver of Premium can be attached.

  1. Buy personal term cover now, sized to household expenses and outstanding personal guarantees rather than declared salary, while age and health are on your side.
  2. Add keyman cover once the company has revenue or a valuation worth protecting.
  3. Put employer-employee cover in place for the team as an early, deliberate retention investment.
  4. Review all three annually, because cover set at seed stage rarely matches the liabilities of a Series A company.
  5. Disclose health, income and business details fully at proposal stage, since complete disclosure is what ensures a smooth claim later.

item.title: Code is no longer scarce: Hostinger’s Auksė Žirgulė on what founders should build instead
item.description: At TechSparks 2026, Hostinger’s VP of Product explained that as building gets easier, customer obsession, trust, and product judgment decide who wins.
item.content:encoded:
A founder in Srinagar recently built a website and an application on Hostinger in very little time. When building software takes that little effort, the question for every business shifts from whether it can build to why anyone would choose what it builds.

That shift was the subject of a fireside chat at TechSparks 2026 in Bengaluru, YourStory’s flagship event. Auksė Žirgulė, VP of Product at Hostinger, spoke to Shradha Sharma, Founder and CEO of YourStory and The Bharat Project, about what happens when every business can build its own software.

From building to running a business

Žirgulė began with how the questions customers bring to Hostinger have changed. Publishing a website was once a hard task for non-technical people, and the company’s vision has been to help everyone succeed online. Now that AI has removed much of that barrier, founders are no longer asking how to build. They are asking how to attract clients, drive revenue and run the business.

Fragmentation is part of the problem. A new founder may buy a domain on one platform, set up email on another, and run campaigns on a third, ending up with five subscriptions and five logins. When something breaks, the founder turns into a technician or integration specialist. Hostinger’s answer is to take care of the full flow and to bring AI agents into it.

Where the advantage lies

If code is no longer scarce, the edge moves to understanding the customer. Founders need to know exactly which problem they are solving and test the product as early as possible. Innovation, Žirgulė argued, does not mean inventing something new. Apple did not invent the mobile phone or the touch screen, yet the iPhone won by delivering the best customer experience.

She also drew on the book ‘Monetizing Innovation’ to make a point many builders forget in their rush to test: a great product does not always make a great business. Thinking about how a product will reach the market has to start early.

That is why she calls customer obsession the thing that should not change. “Customer obsession is the foundation, and I know that now AI is everywhere, but this is the part we need to keep,” she said. She does not mean a survey sent by AI over email, but honest conversations.

Sharma shared a lesson from the Bharat Project’s travels through Bihar, eastern Uttar Pradesh, Assam and Chhattisgarh. The team expected people to respond by email or WhatsApp, but many were watching and observing them on Facebook. Customers, she noted, are not always where a founder assumes they are.

Judgment and trust in the age of agents

As agents take on more decisions, the question is who makes the final call. For now, Žirgulė said, it is still the founder. “AI can do a lot, but the founder says the last word,” she said.

Trust, she added, has to be earned. She shared a story of an agent at Hostinger that agreed to a conference over email, leaving the CEO to learn of his own participation on LinkedIn. Her takeaway was to treat an agent like a new joiner. “I’m looking at this as a new colleague,” she said, which means testing its work and watching how it behaves before giving it more responsibility. That trust is also what worries her most, even as she is excited by how quickly the technology is moving.

Adoption and markets differ

Žirgulė noted that selling approaches vary widely from one market to another, citing India and Brazil, so products have to adapt. Sharma observed that the AI conversation in tech circles can look very different from the world outside them. Žirgulė agreed that adoption cycles differ and that those who are not yet convinced need to be educated on AI’s value.

What the audience asked

Audience questions covered where to stop automating, whether customer expectations will rise, and how non-technical founders can write good prompts. Žirgulė said agents must be tested and observed closely before more is automated, and that rising expectations mean products with strong UX and quality will win.

If launching software as quickly as the Srinagar founder did becomes the norm, the session suggested that what will set businesses apart is knowing the customer, owning the final judgment, and earning trust, whether from a user or an AI agent. Code may no longer be scarce, but those three still are.

item.title: NTT DATA explores expansion in Mangaluru and Udupi, meets Priyank Kharge
item.description: NTT DATA is exploring expansion in Mangaluru and Udupi, with IT Minister Priyank Kharge discussing opportunities in data centres, cloud services, digital infrastructure, biotechnology and startup collaboration.
item.content:encoded:
Karnataka wants its next wave of technology investments to reach beyond Bengaluru, and global IT companies are being encouraged to look towards its coastal cities.

NTT DATA is exploring plans to expand its operations in Karnataka, with Mangaluru and Udupi emerging as potential areas of focus. The company shared its expansion plans during discussions with Karnataka IT, BT and Rural Development Minister Priyank Kharge on November 2, 2026.

The discussions covered new areas of collaboration, technology investments and opportunities to strengthen the company's presence in the state. NTT DATA, which recently acquired Karnataka-based Niveus Solutions and WinWire, cited the availability of skilled talent as a key advantage in expanding its operations, particularly along the coast.

Beyond Bengaluru takes centre stage

Priyank Kharge highlighted the state's Beyond Bengaluru programme, which aims to develop technology ecosystems across Karnataka by extending investments, infrastructure and employment opportunities to emerging technology clusters.

“Through our Beyond Bengaluru programme, we are building strong regional technology ecosystems by investing in skilling, infrastructure and progressive policies. Our focus is on taking investments and opportunities to where the talent is,” he said.

He added that the government wanted to work closely with industry to develop solutions that could accelerate growth across Karnataka's emerging technology hubs.

Data centres, cloud and digital infrastructure on the agenda

The meeting also explored opportunities under Karnataka's Sustainable Data Centre Policy and potential collaboration with NTT DATA across data centres, cloud services and digital infrastructure.

Moreover, Kharge outlined plans for a cable landing station in Mangaluru, which is expected to strengthen the state's digital infrastructure, and discussed how NTT DATA's expertise could support the project.

The minister also encouraged the company to explore opportunities beyond cloud services in sectors such as biotechnology, healthcare, life sciences and automotive manufacturing. These areas align with Karnataka's existing industrial and research ecosystem.

Startup collaboration and new technology opportunities

Startup incubation and innovation were also part of the discussions. Priyank Kharge also mentioned the recently launched Government First programme, which allows startups to pilot their solutions with public sector departments.

He invited NTT DATA to partner with the initiative and contribute to Karnataka's startup ecosystem.

The meeting was attended by senior government officials, including Dr N. Manjula, Secretary, Department of Electronics, IT, BT and S&T; Dr Avinash Menon Rajendran, IAS, Director, Department of Electronics, IT and BT and Managing Director of Karnataka Innovation and Technology Society (KITS); and Sanjeev Gupta, CEO of KDEM.

NTT DATA was represented by Charlie Li, President and Global Head of Cloud, AI and Security; Ayman Husain, Worldwide Managing Director and VP, Google Business Unit; and Shashir Shetty, Chief Growth Officer.

With Mangaluru and Udupi being discussed as potential expansion destinations, Karnataka is looking to extend its technology footprint beyond Bengaluru and bring more specialised technology investments to its coastal region.

item.title: Deeptech startups gain VC attention as India’s investment landscape evolves
item.description: During a panel discussion at TechSparks 2026, an incubator, early stage venture capital firm and a late stage investor provided interesting perspectives on the evolving investment landscape in India, particularly in the areas of artificial intelligence and deeptech.
item.content:encoded:
India’s deeptech startup ecosystem is witnessing growing investor interest, with themes such as technological sovereignty, import substitution, AI infrastructure and advanced manufacturing emerging as key investment opportunities. After years of limited access to early-stage capital, deeptech ventures are increasingly attracting funds willing to back them from the pre-seed stage, signalling a shift in the country’s venture capital landscape.

During a panel discussion at TechSparks 2026, an incubator, early stage venture capital firm and a late stage investor provided interesting perspectives on the evolving investment landscape in India, particularly in the areas of artificial intelligence and deeptech.

Priyanka Agarwal Chopra, Managing Partner and CEO of IIMA Ventures, said deeptech had traditionally been a challenging investment segment because of its high risks and longer gestation periods, which often did not align with conventional venture capital timelines.

“When we started, our founding vision was to address gaps in India's innovation and entrepreneurship ecosystem, particularly in markets and sectors where private sector capital was not available,” she said.

IIMA Ventures was among the early investors in India's deeptech ecosystem, supporting companies in areas that were then categorised as high technology. Chopra said two major themes currently driving deeptech innovation in India are technological sovereignty and import substitution.

She added that while investing in deeptech at the early stages was once a relatively isolated proposition, more funds are now showing interest in supporting companies even at the pre-seed stage.

The growing focus on building indigenous technology capabilities is also creating opportunities for Indian startups to address domestic requirements while developing products for global markets.

Anaina Malik, Partner at VU Venture Partners, said AI infrastructure would be an important investment opportunity as India expands its AI application ecosystem. She emphasised that infrastructure development should receive attention alongside application-led innovation.

Malik also identified agriculture and advanced manufacturing as underserved sectors with considerable potential for technological disruption. She said the firm was looking at startups addressing India's domestic requirements as well as companies building products and solutions for international markets.

According to her, the boundaries between domestic and global markets are increasingly dissolving, with international capital also showing greater interest in investment opportunities emerging from India.

Meanwhile, Sandeep Sinha, Co-founder and Co-CEO of Oister Global, said India's deeptech ecosystem had matured considerably, with several companies that began their journeys eight to 10 years ago now reaching commercial readiness.

He pointed out that many of these ventures had already addressed significant technology and research and development risks and were generating revenues from both domestic and international markets.

Sinha said deeptech companies were increasingly demonstrating the ability to create value through revenue growth, margin expansion and market expansion. The emergence of commercially viable businesses with greater revenue visibility represents an important development for investors evaluating the sector.

While acknowledging that the funding ecosystem remains somewhat fragmented, he described the current activity as 'chaos by design', adding that the increased movement of capital and investors over the past 18-24 months had brought deeptech into sharper focus.

The panellists also highlighted the importance of founder capabilities in determining investment decisions, particularly at the early stages when financial and operating data are limited.

Chopra said investors at the early stage place considerable emphasis on four parameters: founder depth, founder-problem fit, the unique insight of the entrepreneur and the market opportunity.

Sinha, meanwhile, stressed the need for founders to build predictable businesses and diversify their customer base rather than depend excessively on a single customer, irrespective of its importance.

Beyond AI

On investment sizes, Malik said VU Venture Partners' initial cheque sizes remained between $250,000 and $1 million. However, the firm had increased its follow-on investments, choosing to stay invested for longer and support founders through different stages of growth.

She added that evaluating AI startups had become more challenging because of the large number of companies identifying themselves as AI businesses. Consequently, the firm was placing greater emphasis on understanding the underlying technology through deeper due diligence.

Despite the growing investor focus on AI and deeptech, Chopra cautioned entrepreneurs against assuming that opportunities in other sectors had diminished. Consumer businesses, fintech and retail continue to offer substantial opportunities, supported by strong domestic demand.

She emphasised that India's startup ecosystem has room for multiple business models and sectors, and encouraged founders to pursue opportunities they are genuinely passionate about.

item.title: OYO parent PRISM’s revenue rises 35% to Rs 2,814 Cr in Q1 FY27
item.description: PRISM's hotel segment bookings grew 30% year-on-year, while the vacation homes business recorded 28% growth in bookings.
item.content:encoded:
IPO-bound PRISM, parent entity of hospitality chain OYO, has posted a consolidated profit after tax (PAT) of Rs 353 crore in the first quarter ended June, registering 17% growth from Rs 301 crore in the year-ago period.

The quarterly profit included a deferred-tax credit of approximately Rs 244 crore, according to the company's audited financials.

PRISM's revenue from operations increased 35% to Rs 2,814 crore in the first quarter of FY2026-27, compared with Rs 2,078 crore in the corresponding quarter last year, the audited financials showed.

The company's Gross Booking Value grew 30% to nearly Rs 9,600 crore in the same period.

Growth was broad-based across its hotels and vacation homes businesses.

PRISM's hotel segment bookings grew 30% year-on-year, while the vacation homes business recorded 28% growth in bookings.

Addressing shareholders at the company's Extraordinary General Meeting (EGM) in early October, PRISM Founder Ritesh Agarwal said, "What is encouraging is that this momentum has continued into the first quarter of FY27. Our performance across hotels and vacation homes has demonstrated improving gross margins and higher operating earnings, even as we invest in expanding our brands and strengthening customer demand."

"We are continuing to grow our business while generating healthy operating earnings. We are seeing the benefits of the investments we have made over the past few years in technology, brands and distribution capabilities, while continuing to invest quite aggressively," he had said.

In his EGM address, Agarwal highlighted the importance of the company's geographically diversified business, with North America remaining a key market following the acquisition of G6 Hospitality. He said G6 alone contributed approximately Rs 14,000 crore in Gross Booking Value during FY26.

Other profitability indicators also strengthened in the June quarter: EBITDA rose 24% year-on-year to Rs 760 crore, while adjusted EBITDA, net of lease expenses, increased 35% to Rs 589 crore.

Its common technology platform is built centrally and replicated across markets, supporting pricing, distribution, reservations, customer service and property management. PRISM is also embedding AI in pricing and workflows; its Grace AI general manager supports operations at several hotels in Western markets. 

Separately, an October 26 addendum filed with SEBI cut the proposed IPO fresh issue to up to Rs 3,350 crore and earmarked Rs 2,512.5 crore for repayment or prepayment of borrowings through a subsidiary, while removing the proposed pre-IPO placement.

item.title: Customers withdraw $3.6B after largest theft in Binance's history
item.description: According to media reports, customers withdrew $3.6 billion of assets from Binance as it reopened on Sunday following the theft.
item.content:encoded:
Binance witnessed a massive increase in outflows, with customers withdrawing $3.6 billion from the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange after the largest theft in its history, which has been linked to North Korea.

According to media reports, customers withdrew $3.6 billion of assets from Binance as it reopened on Sunday following the theft of $6.3 billion on Thursday.

The company had suspended all transactions following the incident.

"Binance began restoring withdrawals in phases at 06:00 UTC on November 1, 2026," the company posted on X on Sunday, three days after it froze assets in the wake of the theft.

"By 12:36 UTC, withdrawals had resumed for all 15 networks and assets in the initial phase. After an initial spike, withdrawal volumes have declined and are stabilising as expected, while deposit volumes have remained substantial," it said.

According to Binance, customers deposited $1.01 billion and withdrew about $4.649 billion in assets. Most of those transactions occurred in the first few hours after trading was restored, it added.

The outflow of $3.64 billion represents 2.1% of $171 billion in total assets under its management, the company said on Sunday.

"Our team continues testing rigorously the remaining networks and assets. We know how important safe and reliable access to your funds is and will share details of the next phase as soon as we can. Rest assured that market conditions are stable,” Binance said in a post on X.

The company said that it would cover all losses that occurred during the hack and that it had worked with other cryptocurrency firms to freeze about USD 3 billion in stolen assets, according to a The New York Times report.

The paper said that the cybersecurity analysts and the FBI have attributed the theft to North Korea, which has targeted cryptocurrency companies for years, taking advantage of vulnerabilities in their infrastructure to steal assets.

"The hackers may have used artificial intelligence technology to accelerate their attack, according to the crypto analytics firm Chainalysis, which said that the attackers processed 'thousands of transactions in a short period'," the NYT report said.

Changpeng Zhao, a co-founder of Binance, said, "Trust isn’t earned by what you say in good times. It’s earned by what you do in hard times."

According to the NYT, he also warned customers to beware of online scammers making bogus offers of compensation.""

item.title: Startup news and updates: daily roundup (November 02, 2026)
item.description: YourStory presents the daily news roundup from the Indian startup ecosystem and beyond. Here's the roundup for Monday, November 02, 2026.
item.content:encoded:
From AI-powered, full-stack clean energy deployment platform, Two Point O Capital (TW.O), raising $10 million in a funding round led by Transition Venture Capital, to Competition watchdog CCI approving Dutch investment group Prosus' proposal to acquire a stake in Sachin Bansal-led fintech firm Navi, here are the latest developments across sectors.

Featured Stories

Two Point O raises $10M led by Transition Venture Capital

Two Point O Capital (TW.O), an AI-powered, full-stack clean energy deployment platform for commercial and industrial (C&I) businesses, has raised $10 million in a funding round led by Transition Venture Capital. Existing investor Omnivore and angel investors Chiranjeev Singh Saluja and Sudhir M Reddy also participated in the round.

TW.O said it will use the funds to expand into new asset classes, including battery energy storage systems (BESS), and deepen its presence in existing segments such as solar, energy efficiency and wastewater treatment.

Read more

Latest News

Prosus investment in Sachin Bansal's Navi gets CCI nod

Competition watchdog CCI has approved Dutch investment group Prosus' proposal to acquire a stake in Sachin Bansal-led fintech firm Navi Ltd, paving the way for the investment group to deepen its presence in India's digital financial services sector.

"The proposed combination involves the acquisition of certain shareholding in Navi Ltd (target) by MIH Payments Holdings BV (acquirer)," the regulator said in a release. The Competition Commission of India (CCI) said it has approved the proposed deal.

Read more

Funding News

ValueQuest Tristar Fund raises over Rs 2,100 Cr for advanced manufacturing

ValueQuest Tristar Fund, a private equity fund that backs India’s advanced manufacturing sector, has received more than Rs 2,100 crore in commitments from investors. It reached this within 15 months of its first close, beating both its original target and the full greenshoe (the extra amount a fund is allowed to raise above its target).

The fund invests in aerospace, defence, precision engineering and manufacturing linked to the energy transition.

Read more

Other News

Razorpay Wins Final IFSCA Licence to Run Cross-Border Money Movement from GIFT City

Razorpay has received its final Payment Service Provider licence from the IFSCA, following in-principle approval in April 2026. The licence lets it move money in and out of India from GIFT City under a single regulatory framework. 

Its infrastructure supports global investing, international collections, settlements and multi-currency accounts, with banking integrations live with RBL Bank and ICICI Bank. Investment platforms can integrate once, cutting timelines from months to two to three weeks. The move responds to rising demand, as Indian residents put $2.65 billion into overseas stocks and debt in FY26, up 56 per cent year on year.

Arrowhead AI launches Fletch, a voice model built for India and Southeast Asia's multilingual conversations

Arrowhead AI, a Bengaluru-based voice AI company, has launched Fletch, an in-house text-to-speech model for multilingual customer calls. It supports 14 languages, switches between them mid-sentence and offers 12 emotion styles. Fletch reports 80 milliseconds of latency and starts speaking in under 100 milliseconds. 

Already powering over one million calls a day for clients such as Axis Bank and RBL Bank, it claims roughly 30% better pronunciation accuracy on selected names and terms, a figure the company stresses is not an overall call-resolution gain. Arrowhead is adding Malay and Indonesian support ahead of Singapore FinTech Festival 2026.

BikeWo Green Tech signs MoU with Eden Green Energy to explore electric mobility opportunities

BikeWo Green Tech Limited has signed a strategic Memorandum of Understanding with Eden Green Energy Private Limited to explore collaboration in electric mobility and sustainable transportation. The companies will look at opportunities in EV fleet solutions, vehicle leasing, charging infrastructure, and workforce, rider and operational management. 

BikeWo brings expertise in leasing, infrastructure and business development, while Eden contributes workforce and operational strengths. Eden's Managing Director said the partnership aligns with plans to expand dedicated electric fleets and charging networks in Tamil Nadu, including Chennai and Tiruchirappalli. Both firms aim to build scalable, zero-emission mobility solutions.

Fibe launches UPI payments on its App after NPCI third-party provider approval

Digital lending platform Fibe has launched its UPI offering following NPCI approval to operate as a Third-Party Application Provider. The service is open to consumers across India, including those who are not existing Fibe customers. Users can pay through bank accounts, RuPay Credit Cards and eligible credit lines, all within a single UPI experience. 

The launch adds an everyday payments layer to Fibe's range of products, which includes the Fibe Axis Bank Credit Card, third-party FDs and Loan Against Mutual Funds. Group CEO Akshay Mehrotra said the aim is to give users greater choice, control and value in every transaction.

DHL Express appoints Sandeep Juneja to lead South Asia and India business

DHL Express has appointed Sandeep Juneja as Senior Vice President for South Asia and Managing Director for India, effective 1 November 2026. He succeeds R. S. Subramanian, who moves to Blue Dart as Managing Director. Juneja joined DHL Express in 2004, has sat on the India Management Board since 2007 and has led the commercial function since 2013. 

He will focus on customer partnerships, people and sustainable growth, and will also oversee Nepal, Bhutan, the Maldives, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh. Asia Pacific CEO Ken Lee said Juneja brings the market knowledge and customer relationships needed for the next phase of growth.

Nagaland University-led study proposes framework to evaluate AI tools for preserving India's cultural heritage

A research team led by Nagaland University, with scholars from institutions in Tamil Nadu, Delhi, Uttar Pradesh, Telangana and Karnataka, has proposed a framework to evaluate how AI can help preserve manuscripts, endangered languages, oral traditions and historical records. It assesses tools across nine areas, including text recognition, translation, cultural context and ethics, combining technical checks with expert and community review.

The researchers stress that AI should support, not replace, archivists, linguists and cultural custodians, since technical accuracy does not guarantee cultural accuracy. They recommend piloting the framework across different collections, scripts and dialects. The findings appear in Acta Innovations.

Thyrocare launches India's first pregnancy kit with bundled lab confirmation test; Yami Gautam named brand ambassador

Thyrocare Technologies has entered the pregnancy testing segment with the Thyrocare Pregnancy Kit, which it says is India's first to include a quantitative laboratory confirmation. Priced at Rs 60, the kit contains a rapid at-home test and a voucher for a Beta hCG blood test at Rs 399, half the regular Rs 800, with home sample collection included. 

Users book the test by scanning a QR code, and the voucher is valid for six months. Actor Yami Gautam is the brand ambassador. Thyrocare's MD and CEO Rahul Guha said the kit pairs a quick home answer with clinical confirmation.

ICICI Lombard's Startup Shield forum helps Bengaluru startups build resilience against emerging business risks

ICICI Lombard General Insurance hosted "Startup Shield – The Risk Readiness Forum" in Bengaluru on 27 October 2026 to help startups prepare for emerging risks. Karnataka has 24,026 DPIIT-recognised startups, and the discussions covered AI-driven threats, cyber and data security, employee wellness, professional indemnity, directors and officers liability, asset protection and business interruption. 

Founders, investors, CXOs and risk professionals attended, and ICICI Lombard experts shared real-world case studies. Anand Singhi, the company's Chief for Corporate, International, Banca and Government Business, said risk preparedness is increasingly a marker of business maturity that influences how investors and enterprise partners assess a company.

Avendus appoints Sumit Agarwal as Managing Director and Head of Equity Corporate Finance

Avendus has appointed Sumit Agarwal as Managing Director and Head of Equity Corporate Finance, Investment Banking, reporting to Karan Sharma, Head of Investment Banking at Avendus Capital. He will lead the firm's equity capital markets execution, strengthening its ability to deliver end-to-end IPO mandates and follow-on offerings. 

Agarwal has over 18 years of experience and has led more than 100 transactions, including IPOs, FPOs, QIPs, InvITs and rights issues. He joins from Kotak Mahindra Capital and previously worked at ICICI Securities. Sharma said Agarwal brings deep execution expertise and strong institutional relationships that will broaden the firm's ECM capabilities.

Xflow launches SaaS subscription management tool for businesses to pay global vendors like AWS and OpenAI

Cross-border payments company Xflow has launched SaaS Subscription Management, letting businesses pay and track global subscriptions such as AWS, OpenAI, Figma and Slack in one place. Companies pay Xflow via SWIFT in USD or through NEFT/RTGS in INR, and use a USD virtual card for all subscription payments. 

The tool addresses failed recurring payments on domestic cards and scattered renewals across teams and currencies. CEO Ashwin Bhatnagar cited industry estimates that over 30 per cent of card-based recurring payments fail in India, and said Xflow is already processing millions in volume since launch. Blume Ventures' Amit Gajaria praised the service.
