item.title: Ambani tops Forbes' global billionaire gainers list with $7B wealth jump as Reliance shares soar
item.description: The gains pushed Ambani to No.23 spot on the world billionaire list, making him the richest Indian ahead of Gautam Adani, who was ranked at No.26.
item.content:encoded:
Reliance Industries chairman Mukesh Ambani has emerged as the world's biggest billionaire wealth gainer, adding over $6 billion to his fortune in a single day, as shares of his flagship company surged following a stronger-than-expected quarterly earnings performance.

According to Forbes' Real-Time Billionaires list, Ambani's wealth increased by 7.85%, or $6.3 billion, making him the biggest gainer globally in the latest update to the ranking on November 2.

The gain was substantially ahead of the second-biggest wealth accretion on the list, with Spanish retail billionaire Amancio Ortega adding $1.7 billion, followed by China's Zhong Shanshan at $1.5 billion.

The gains pushed Ambani to No.23 spot on the world billionaire list, making him the richest Indian ahead of Gautam Adani, who was ranked at No.26 with a wealth of $79.12 billion, according to the Forbes listing. Ambani had a wealth of $88.8 billion, according to Forbes.

The sharp increase in Ambani's wealth coincided with a rally in Reliance Industries shares, which jumped 11.6% on Monday, marking their strongest trading session in more than six years. The stock closed at its day's high and was the biggest gainer on the benchmark Nifty 50 index.

The rally followed Reliance's September-quarter results, which showed a 40.6% year-on-year increase in consolidated net profit to Rs 25,548 crore, significantly ahead of analyst expectations. Stronger refining and petrochemical margins, alongside improved profitability at its telecom business Jio, helped drive the earnings growth.

The results reinforced investor confidence in Reliance's two major earnings engines - its oil-to-chemicals business and digital services - even as profitability in its retail business remained under pressure.

The company's refining core earnings surged 68%, while Jio Platforms' core earnings rose 16.6% during the quarter.

"Mukesh Ambani chairs and runs $125 billion (revenue) Reliance Industries, which has interests in petrochemicals, oil and gas, telecom, retail, media and financial services," Forbes said.

Reliance was founded by his late father Dhirubhai Ambani, a yarn trader, in 1966 as a small textile manufacturer. After his father's death in 2002, Ambani and his younger sibling, Anil, divided the family empire.

Reliance's telecom and broadband service Jio Platforms got listed in October 2026, achieving a market capitalisation of $137 billion, which made it the country's second-most valuable company after its parent.

Ambani's three children joined the board of Reliance in 2023. Son Akash heads Jio; daughter Isha oversees retail and financial services; and younger son Anant is in the energy business.

In 2026, Ambani announced plans for a $110 billion investment in AI infrastructure to be built across the country over the next seven years, the publication added.""

item.title: ValueQuest Tristar Fund raises over Rs 2,100 Cr for advanced manufacturing
item.description: The private equity fund, which focuses on aerospace, defence, precision engineering and energy-transition-linked manufacturing, has secured commitments exceeding its original target and full greenshoe within 15 months of its first close.
item.content:encoded:
ValueQuest Tristar Fund, a private equity fund that backs India’s advanced manufacturing sector, has received more than Rs 2,100 crore in commitments from investors. It reached this within 15 months of its first close, beating both its original target and the full greenshoe (the extra amount a fund is allowed to raise above its target).

The fund invests in aerospace, defence, precision engineering and manufacturing linked to the energy transition.

So far, it has backed four companies: Hi-Q Electronics makes critical circuit boards for aerospace and defence. Rangsons Aerospace builds fluid distribution systems and satellite communications equipment. Waaree Energy Storage Solutions focuses on battery energy storage. Trusted Aerospace & Engineers (TASE Global) is a precision engineering firm that serves several industries and manufactures across borders.

To pick its investments, the fund combines in-depth sector research with a mapping of industrial value chains. This helps the fund find specialised manufacturers that stand to gain from long-term industry growth and from key turning points in their own businesses.

“India is at the beginning of a multi-decade transformation in advanced manufacturing. But sector growth alone does not guarantee investment returns. The real differentiator is identifying the right businesses at the right stage of their evolution. The work we do upfront gives us the conviction to partner with strong promoters and deepen our exposure as they deliver against milestones,” said Aniket Dharamshi, Co-Founder and Managing Partner, ValueQuest Investment Advisors.

“In advanced manufacturing, competitive advantage is built over years through process expertise, rigorous customer qualification and consistent delivery on quality and reliability. Once a supplier becomes integral to a customer’s critical programs, replacing it can involve significant time, cost and execution risk. We seek businesses that can build on these capabilities to deepen customer relationships and translate industry growth into sustained, profitable growth,” said Dr. Arvind Ananthanarayanan, Partner, ValueQuest Private Equity.

ValueQuest Private Equity is also raising its SCALE Fund II, which will invest in established businesses with clear competitive advantages and visible routes to an exit for investors.

ValueQuest Private Equity is the private equity arm of ValueQuest Investment Advisors. It manages over Rs 6,000 crore across two investment strategies, three funds and co-investments. ValueQuest Investment Advisors manages about $3.4 billion across public and private markets.

item.title: How Zocket is building the brain behind enterprise marketing
item.description: As frontier models become interchangeable, the ET Enterprise AI Award-winning startup is betting that its Brand Brain, a context layer that knows each brand’s customers, voice, and performance history, is what will set enterprise marketers apart.
item.content:encoded:
For the last three years, enterprise AI has been told one story: pick the most powerful model and you win. Every launch brought a new benchmark, a bigger context window, and a sharper reasoning score. Boardrooms debated which model to bet on as if it were a once-in-a-decade infrastructure decision.

That story is running out of road. The gap between the leading models is narrowing every quarter, and most enterprises can now access near-frontier intelligence through a single API call. When everyone has access to the same brain, the brain stops being the advantage.

The next battle in enterprise AI will be won in context: the proprietary knowledge, history, signals and judgement that tell a model what your business actually needs. Models are becoming the engine. Context is becoming the fuel, the map and the destination.

The model is becoming a commodity

Consider how quickly the landscape has shifted. A capability that felt magical 18 months ago, such as summarizing a 100-page contract or writing production-ready code, is now table stakes across multiple providers. Open-weight models have closed much of the gap with proprietary ones. Inference costs keep falling. Switching from one model to another, once a painful migration, is increasingly a configuration change.

This is the classic arc of any foundational technology. Electricity, cloud computing and bandwidth all followed it: a period of scarcity and differentiation, followed by abundance and standardization. Nobody today wins because they have a better power supply. They win because of what they build on top of it.

For enterprise leaders, the implication is uncomfortable but liberating. If your AI strategy rests mainly on which model you chose, your competitors can replicate it in a weekend. A durable advantage has to come from somewhere else.

What ‘context’ really means

AI models are powerful, but intelligence alone is not enough to understand how an enterprise operates. What makes AI genuinely useful is the context surrounding every decision: the brand, its customers, its business priorities, and the processes that govern how work gets done.

For enterprise marketing, context goes beyond feeding information into a model. It means connecting four critical layers of intelligence:

Data context: Customer behavior, campaign performance, product information, consumer interactions, and historical trends. These signals help AI understand what is working, what is changing, and where opportunities exist.

Brand and institutional context: Brand guidelines, tone of voice, positioning, compliance requirements, past decisions, and business priorities. This is the knowledge that ensures every AI-generated action reflects the organization it represents.

Workflow context: Understanding how marketing operates across teams, from creative development and campaign execution to approvals, governance, and reporting. AI needs to recognize not just what to do, but how decisions move through an organization.

Real-time context: Consumer sentiment, emerging market trends, competitor activity, and live campaign performance. This allows AI to respond to changing conditions rather than relying entirely on historical information.

The challenge is that most AI tools operate with only fragments of this intelligence. A creative tool may understand brand guidelines but lack campaign performance data. A media platform may optimize spending without understanding consumer sentiment. A research tool may identify emerging trends without connecting those insights to the next marketing decision.

The result is fragmented intelligence across an increasingly connected marketing ecosystem.

This is where Zocket's Brand Brain introduces a different approach. Rather than treating every marketing function as an isolated AI workflow, Brand Brain brings brand knowledge, consumer intelligence, performance signals, and governance into a shared context layer that powers specialised AI marketing capabilities.

The underlying principle is simple: AI becomes more valuable when it understands not just the task it has been asked to perform, but the business behind it. For enterprises, that is the shift from AI that generates outputs to AI that can support informed, consistent, and connected marketing decisions at scale.

Why context is the moat that lasts

Models can be bought. Context has to be built, and that is precisely why it is defensible.

First, context is proprietary by nature. No competitor can download your ten years of customer interactions or the hard-won lessons of your last hundred campaigns. Second, context compounds. Every decision an AI system makes, and every outcome it observes, becomes a new context that sharpens the next decision. An organization that starts capturing this loop today will be meaningfully ahead of one that starts in two years.

Third, context is hard. In most enterprises, valuable knowledge is scattered across CRMs, spreadsheets, ad platforms, email threads and the heads of a few senior employees. It is siloed, inconsistently labelled, and often outdated. Getting it into a form an AI system can reliably use requires investment in data infrastructure, governance and integration, work that is unglamorous but decisive.

This is why so many enterprise AI pilots look impressive in a demo and disappoint in production. The model was rarely the problem. The missing piece was context: the system simply did not know enough about the business to make the right call.

"Enterprises often ask us which model is best. The better question is how quickly your systems can turn scattered data into something an AI can trust and act on. The model is the easy part to swap. The context layer, with its integrations, retrieval and feedback loops, is what takes real engineering, and it is where performance is won or lost," says Mukund Srivathsan, Co-founder and CTO, Zocket

Also Read
The Zocket Story: Building Brand Brain, the context and orchestration layer for AI-native enterprise marketing

A view from marketing and advertising

At Zocket, this shift is seen most clearly in marketing, where AI adoption has been fast and the cost of generic output is immediately visible.

Any model today can generate an ad headline, a product description or a campaign plan in seconds. But a generic headline is not a good headline. A good one reflects the brand's voice, speaks to a specific audience segment, learns from which creatives converted last month and adapts to what is trending on each platform this week.

The difference between an ad that performs and one that burns budget is almost never the raw writing ability of the model. It is the context behind the prompt.

The same is true for budget allocation, audience targeting, and performance optimization. An AI agent that understands a brand's historical cost per acquisition, its seasonal patterns, its margins and its competitive landscape will consistently outperform a more powerful model working blind. The biggest gains for marketers come not from upgrading the model but from enriching what the model knows.

This is why Zocket believes the future of AI in marketing is agentic and context-rich: systems that continuously learn from a brand's own data and outcomes, rather than tools that start from zero with every request.

"Every brand now has access to the same AI. What it does not have is the same understanding of its customers. Our focus at Zocket is helping businesses turn their own data and results into an AI that gets smarter about them every single day. That is the advantage nobody can copy,” says Karthik Venkateswaran, Co-founder and CEO, Zocket

What enterprise leaders should do now

If context is the new battleground, the playbook changes. Five priorities stand out.

Treat context as a strategic asset. Audit where your most valuable knowledge lives and who owns it. Customer data, performance history, and institutional rules deserve the same rigour as financial data.

Stay model-agnostic. Build architectures that let you swap models as the market evolves. Lock-in to a single model is a risk; lock-in to your own context is an advantage.

Close the feedback loop. Design AI systems that capture outcomes, not just outputs. Knowing which recommendation worked, and why, is what makes context compound over time.

Invest in the plumbing. Data integration, retrieval systems, governance, and access controls are not back-office chores. They are the foundation of AI performance.

Encode judgement, not just data. Capture the rules, guardrails, and preferences your best people apply instinctively, so AI can apply them consistently at scale.

The winners will be the ones who know the most

The first chapter of enterprise AI was about access: who could get their hands on capable models and put them to work. That chapter is almost at an end. The next one will be about understanding whose AI knows their customers, their markets, and their own business most deeply.

In that world, the question in the boardroom shifts from "Which model are we using?" to "What does our AI know that nobody else does?" The companies with a compelling answer, built on rich, connected, and continuously improving context, will set the pace for their industries.

Models will keep getting better, and that is good news for everyone. But because they are getting better for everyone, they cannot be what sets you apart. Context can. The enterprises that start building it seriously today will not just use AI more effectively. They will own an advantage that no model upgrade can buy.

item.title: How the open-source route helped Uzair Ali land global roles
item.description: Open source was not a shortcut for this young techie to land an interview or a job; it was a proactive way to make his work speak for himself.
item.content:encoded:
Indian engineers no longer have to relocate abroad or go through several rounds of resume screening and interviews to bag global roles. Increasingly, open-source public code is paving the way for that.

Public code is a record anyone can read and inspect, and hiring teams are actively using it to assess one's real-world engineering skills. It includes open-source contributions, public repositories (like GitHub), and code samples that hiring managers can evaluate.

This is how Uzair Ali landed internships at various global companies and eventually became a founding engineer at a US-based fintech startup.

As a college student at the Kalinga Institute of Industrial Technology in Bhubaneswar, Ali was building a tool to monitor server logs. He shared his repository of work in open source on X, which caught the attention of the CTO of Dukaan, an Indian mobile-first, do-it-yourself ecommerce platform, leading to an interview at the firm.

Ali joined Dukaan as a backend intern in January 2022 in Bengaluru.

This was an early lesson in the value of making his work visible to the world. It helped his project reach someone who might otherwise have not seen his resume.

Ali's career path did not follow a straight line through a typical hiring funnel at big tech companies.

After a stint at Dukaan, he interned at HackerRank and FamPay while still being in university. After graduating, he joined Civo, a London-based cloud infrastructure provider.

Twenty-four-year-old Ali is now an engineer at Flip Laboratories, a San Francisco-based fintech startup. He works from India.

In an interaction with YourStory, Ali says all his career moves from being a backend engineer to AI work and now to being part of the founding team at Flip are largely thanks to his open-source contributions.

Ali reasons that open-source code helps software maintainers see how people works over months, while the reviews show how they handle feedback.

Now anyone with an internet connection can pick a project, fix what is broken, and receive feedback and reviews. Over time, this history builds a credible repository of one's work in a way a resume cannot, says the techie.

Ali's GitHub profile has a number of pull requests merged in various open source projects such as LiteLLM, a widely used open-source LLM gateway.

A pull request is a request from others to merge a code into their projects, and this is reveiwed jointly by those who create the code and those who would like to integrate it.

Ali's most visible work is on Agno, an open-source framework for building AI agents. It has more than 42,000 stars on GitHub. He also has contributions in major codebases including Terraform, Crossplane, and IntelOwl.

A codebase is a complete compendium of source code, configuration files, and supporting resources used to build, test, and run a software system or application.

Today, Ali is part of the founding team at Flip Laboratories, which has built Flip, a proactive AI agent to manage the finances of Americans. Flip acts like a personal finance assistant operating directly inside users' messaging apps (such as iMessage).

The startup recently raised a $1.4 million pre-seed round from investors including a16z speedrun, Pear VC, The House Fund, and Cory Levy.

For Ali, the thread connecting all his experiences—as a student developer, an intern building cloud tools and an AI framework, and as a founding engineer at a startup—is work that other people can see.

Open source was not a shortcut to an interview or a job; it was a proactive way to make his learning and work visible beyond his college, city, and country.

item.title: Clinics On Cloud raises $12.5M to expand microclinic network
item.description: The Pune-based firm will use the funding to strengthen its artificial intelligence capabilities, expand research and development, and grow its connected microclinic network.
item.content:encoded:
Healthtech company Clinics On Cloud has raised $12.5 million in Series A funding from Dubai-based Model42, a health and wellness growth platform powered by Enlightened Minds Investments.

The Pune-based firm said it will use the funding to strengthen its artificial intelligence capabilities, expand research and development, and grow its connected microclinic network. It also plans partnerships with healthcare providers and technology companies to integrate new screening tools and AI applications. 

The United Arab Emirates will be its global hub, with planned expansion into Africa, the United States and Southeast Asia.

Founded in 2018, Clinics On Cloud builds technology-enabled healthcare access points. Its Health ATMs are compact screening stations combining connected medical devices, health checks and digital reports, alongside AI-assisted insights and telemedicine. Its portfolio also includes Health Lounges, Box Clinics and Mobile Medical Units for hospitals, workplaces, housing communities and underserved areas.

Founder and chief executive officer Abhay Agarwal said the company had spent eight years guided by the belief that “quality healthcare should never depend on someone’s PIN code”. The investment, he said, would help take that vision overseas, with the opportunity lying in “making these innovations accessible to people, wherever they are”.

Clinics On Cloud claims more than 3,500 deployments, over 12 million health screenings and operations in eight countries. Its systems have been used in government health centres, hospitals, corporate sites, rural communities and Indian defence establishments, including the Army, Navy and Border Security Force.

The funding comes amid a more selective investment climate. Venture Intelligence data showed Indian health-tech startup funding fell to $447 million in 2025 from $707 million in 2024. 

However, capital continues to flow into specialised models. In October, preventive-health startup Cent raised $15 million in a Series A led by Blume Ventures and South Park Commons. In July, radiology AI company CARPL.ai secured $10 million in a round led by the International Finance Corporation.

Meanwhile, public digital infrastructure is also expanding. By May 2026, the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission had crossed 90 crore digital health accounts and 100 crore linked health records. Initiatives announced in June, including digital clinic-management tools and common data standards, aim to make health information easier to exchange.

item.title: MobiKwik posts Rs 11.83 Cr profit in Q2 of FY27
item.description: MobiKwik’s revenue grew 9.4% in Q2 FY27, driven by higher gross merchandise value (GMV) and improved margins.
item.content:encoded:
MobiKwik reported a net profit in the second quarter of FY27, compared with a loss in the year-ago period, marking its fourth consecutive profitable quarter and its highest-ever quarterly profit.

The fintech company posted a net profit of Rs 11.83 crore for the July-September quarter, against a loss of Rs 28.61 crore in Q2 FY26.

Revenue rose 9.4% year-on-year (YoY) to Rs 295.70 crore. MobiKwik attributed the quarter’s performance to higher gross merchandise value (GMV) growth and improved margins.

“We believe that the operating leverage in our business model will compound as we evolve into an AI-first company. Our continued focus on cost optimisation and operating efficiency is further strengthening our operating model and will drive profitability as we scale,” said Bipin Preet Singh, MD & CEO, MobiKwik.

According to MobiKwik, its payment business recorded a 35% year-on-year (YoY) growth in gross merchandise value (GMV) to Rs 59,677 crore in Q2 FY27. Consumer payments GMV grew 27% YoY to Rs 46,375 crore, while lending disbursals rose 34% to Rs 1,082.6 crore during the quarter.

The company’s registered user base increased to 196.3 million in Q2 FY27, compared with 183.5 million in the corresponding quarter last fiscal.

MobiKwik is also accelerating the adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) across engineering, lending, customer experience, and risk management. According to the company, AI now generates 92% of its code, helping accelerate go-to-market initiatives by 55%. Its Help LLM resolves 91% of customer queries, while fraud detection is entirely AI-led.

The fintech company added that its AI-powered collections platform facilitates 55% of early collections and has improved collection rates by 33%. Voice AI has also helped achieve 30-40% higher customer connect rates.
